title: The Temple's Fall and the Coming of the Son of Man
summary: Leaving the temple, Jesus predicts that its buildings will be torn down, and on the Mount of Olives the disciples ask when this will happen and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age. He warns of deceivers, wars, persecution, and a great tribulation linked to Daniel's abomination of desolation, and speaks of the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and glory. He says no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son, and calls his followers to keep watch and to be found faithful, like a servant whose master may return at any time.
story:
Jesus has just pronounced that Jerusalem's house will be left desolate (23:38) and has walked out of the temple for the last time. Now, looking back across the Kidron Valley from the Mount of Olives, the mountain where Zechariah had seen the LORD standing on the day of his coming (Zechariah 14:4), he begins the last of the five great teaching blocks in Matthew, known as the Olivet discourse, which runs through chapter 25 and closes with the formula at 26:1. Matthew follows Mark 13 closely through verse 36, then adds sayings found in other settings in Luke (Luke 17:22-37, 12:39-46) and, in chapter 25, three parables of his own.

Here the Gospel's story of Jesus' rejection by Jerusalem's leaders meets the larger story of God's judgment and the end of history. After the discourse the passion narrative begins (26:1-2). The chapter prepares the disciples for a world in which Jesus is absent, the temple falls, and they must bear witness under pressure until he comes. It also looks ahead to the Gospel's last line, where the risen Jesus promises to be with them always, ‘to the end of the age’ (28:20), the same phrase the disciples use in verse 3.
historical:
The temple the disciples admired was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple, begun around 20 or 19 BC and still being finished in the early 60s AD, famous for its white stone and gold (Josephus, Jewish War 5.184-227). The generation after Jesus lived through the events his words describe, and Josephus, who watched the end from the Roman side, is the chief witness. Popular prophets promised signs of deliverance: Theudas around AD 45 (Antiquities 20.97-98), an Egyptian who gathered a crowd on the Mount of Olives in the 50s (Antiquities 20.169-172, Acts 21:38), and others who led people into the wilderness (Jewish War 2.259-263), which fits the warning in verse 26 not to go out when told the Christ is in the wilderness. Famine struck Judea under Claudius (Acts 11:28), an earthquake leveled Laodicea in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27), and Nero turned on the Christians of Rome in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44).

The revolt began in AD 66. The Syrian legate Cestius Gallus marched on Jerusalem that autumn and withdrew with heavy losses; Vespasian subdued Galilee and much of Judea in 67 and 68; after the civil wars of 69 his son Titus besieged the city in the spring of 70. Inside the walls rival factions fought each other. In the winter of 67 to 68 the Zealots made the temple their fortress, chose a high priest by lot, a villager named Phanni who hardly knew what the office was, and defiled the sanctuary with bloodshed (Jewish War 4.151-157). Josephus says an ancient oracle foretold that the city would be taken and the sanctuary burned when sedition came and Jewish hands polluted the temple (Jewish War 4.388). On the day the temple burned, a false prophet had told the people to go up to the temple courts to receive signs of deliverance, and some six thousand died in a burning colonnade (Jewish War 6.283-287). Josephus dates the burning to the tenth of the month Lous (Jewish War 6.250), and Jewish tradition remembers both destructions on the ninth of Av (m. Taanit 4:6). Afterward the Roman soldiers set their standards in the temple court opposite the eastern gate and sacrificed to them (Jewish War 6.316). In his preface Josephus wrote that the misfortunes of all peoples since the world began fall short of those of the Jews in this war (Jewish War 1.12), language close to verse 21, which itself echoes Daniel 12:1.

The phrase ‘the abomination of desolation’ comes from Daniel (9:27, 11:31, 12:11). Its first fulfillment was remembered by every Jew: in December 167 BC Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar on the altar of burnt offering (1 Maccabees 1:54, 1:59). Candidates for what Matthew's readers were to watch for include Pilate's attempt to bring standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem (Antiquities 18.55-59); Caligula's order in AD 40 to set up his statue in the temple, withdrawn before his death (Antiquities 18.261-309; Philo, Embassy to Gaius); the Zealots' profanation of 67 to 68; the Roman armies surrounding the city, as Luke's parallel puts it (Luke 21:20); and the standards and sacrifices of 70. Jerome, writing in 398, added the equestrian statue of Hadrian that in his day stood where the holy of holies had been (Commentary on Matthew, on 24:15), and many interpreters since Irenaeus have looked to a future Antichrist (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4).

Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by an oracle, left the city before the war and settled at Pella, east of the Jordan (Ecclesiastical History 3.5.3), which suggests that the church read verse 16 as a warning to heed. Historians debate how much of the Pella story is history. Messianic claims did not end with the war: in AD 132 Simon bar Kosiba led a second revolt, and the Jerusalem Talmud remembers Rabbi Akiva hailing him as King Messiah, the star out of Jacob of Numbers 24:17 (y. Taanit 4), while another sage answered that grass would grow from Akiva's cheeks before the son of David came.
cultural:
The discourse speaks in the idiom of Jewish apocalyptic, the way of writing about God's decisive acts that runs from Daniel through works such as 1 Enoch and, after AD 70, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch. Verse 29 weaves together Isaiah 13:10, spoken against Babylon, and Isaiah 34:4, spoken against Edom; the prophets used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of empires within history. The mourning of ‘all the tribes of the earth’ in verse 30 echoes Zechariah 12:10-14, where the clans of Israel mourn for the one they pierced (the Hebrew can mean the tribes of the land), a text John and Revelation also apply to Jesus (John 19:37, Revelation 1:7). The Son of Man coming on the clouds is Daniel 7:13-14. The loud trumpet recalls Isaiah 27:13, where a great trumpet gathers the scattered to worship in Jerusalem, and the gathering from the four winds recalls Zechariah 2:6 and Deuteronomy 30:4, where it is God who gathers his exiles. First hearers would neither take such language as a weather report nor dismiss it as ornament; it announced that God was acting in a way that shook the world.

Other images drew on ordinary life. Birth pains were a prophetic picture of the anguish before deliverance (Isaiah 26:17-18, 66:7-9). Flat roofs, reached by outside stairs, were used for work and sleep, so a man on the roof could flee without entering the house; a field worker left his cloak at the field's edge. Pregnant and nursing women suffered most in flight and siege (Lamentations 4:10). Winter rains flooded the wadis and made travel hard. Only Matthew adds the Sabbath (verse 20): Jewish custom limited travel on the Sabbath to a short distance (Acts 1:12 measures the Mount of Olives as a Sabbath day's walk from the city), gates might be shut, and flight on that day would trouble the consciences of observant Jewish believers. First Maccabees tells of pious Jews who let themselves be slaughtered on the Sabbath rather than fight, and of the decision that followed to defend themselves on that day (1 Maccabees 2:32-41).

The saying about the carcass and the vultures (verse 28) was proverbial; Job says of the eagle that where the slain are, there it is (Job 39:30). The Greek aetos can mean eagle or vulture, and some interpreters have seen an allusion to the eagles on the Roman legions' standards, though the proverb needs no such key: where there is death, the birds gather, and the coming of the Son of Man will be as unmistakable. Grinding grain with a hand mill was daily women's work, often done by two women facing each other (compare Exodus 11:5). Roman reckoning divided the night into four watches, which Matthew uses elsewhere (14:25). A thief ‘broke into’ a house literally by digging through (diorussō) its mud-brick wall. A large household had a steward, often himself a slave, set over the other servants to give them their rations at the proper time, the phrase the psalms use of God feeding his creatures (Psalm 104:27, 145:15). Matthew places the wicked servant ‘with the hypocrites’ (verse 51), linking the parable to the woes of chapter 23, where Luke has ‘with the unbelievers’ (Luke 12:46).
literary:
The discourse answers a question in verse 3 that Matthew phrases in three parts: when will these things happen, what will be the sign of your coming (parousia), and what will be the sign of the end of the age. Mark's disciples ask only about the temple (Mark 13:4); Matthew's link the temple's fall to Jesus' coming and the end, and how the answer is divided between them is the main interpretive question. The speech moves from general warnings (verses 4 to 14), to a specific crisis in Judea (15 to 28), to the coming of the Son of Man (29 to 31), to the lesson of the fig tree and the saying about this generation (32 to 35). Verse 36 then turns: ‘No one knows about that day or hour.’ Several interpreters, R. T. France among them, see the turn from the plural ‘those days’ (verses 19, 22, 29) to the singular ‘that day’ as marking a shift from the temple's fall to the final coming. From there to the end of chapter 25 the discourse becomes a series of parables about readiness: Noah's generation, the two in the field and at the mill, the thief in the night, the faithful and wicked servants, and then the ten virgins, the talents, and the sheep and the goats.

Matthew shapes Mark's material in telling ways. He has already used Mark's warnings about councils and governors in the mission discourse (10:17-22), so here he summarizes persecution briefly and adds his own concerns: false prophets (verse 11), the multiplication of lawlessness (anomia, verse 12), the love of most growing cold, and the promise that ‘this gospel of the kingdom’ will be preached in all the world before the end (verse 14). He uses the word parousia four times (verses 3, 27, 37, 39), the only Gospel to use it at all, and the connective ‘then’ (tote) runs through the discourse, with ‘immediately after’ in verse 29 tying the cosmic signs to the tribulation just described.

The chapter is also tied to what surrounds it. Jesus' last public words were ‘your house is left to you desolate’ (23:38), and the discourse begins with the disciples admiring that house. ‘All these things will come upon this generation’ (23:36) is answered by ‘this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened’ (verse 34). Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem's children (23:37); the Son of Man will gather his elect (verse 31), with the same verb. And the command to watch (grēgoreite, verse 42) will be repeated in Gethsemane, where the disciples sleep (26:38-41).

outline.t: The temple's destruction foretold and the disciples' question
The beginning of birth pains: deception, war, persecution, and witness
The abomination of desolation and the great tribulation
The coming of the Son of Man
The lesson of the fig tree
No one knows the day or hour: keep watch
The faithful servant and the wicked servant

doctrines.note: The Son of Man will come ‘on the clouds of heaven, with power and great glory’ and gather his elect (verses 30 and 31), visibly and unmistakably, like lightning from east to west (verse 27). Whatever readers conclude about which verses describe AD 70, the church confesses from this chapter and others that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and verse 36 insists that the day is known to the Father alone.

Jesus foretells the destruction of the temple the disciples admire (verse 2), as Jeremiah and Micah had foretold the fall of the first (Jeremiah 7:12-14, Micah 3:12). In Matthew's story the temple's end follows its leaders' rejection of Jesus (23:38), and the one who is greater than the temple (12:6) is himself the place where God is now with his people (1:23, 18:20, 28:20).

‘The one who perseveres to the end will be saved’ (verse 13). The chapter names what threatens endurance, deception, persecution, betrayal, lawlessness, and love growing cold, and it promises that God shortens the days for the sake of the elect (verse 22) and that false christs will not deceive them ‘if that were possible’ (verse 24). Christians differ on whether the elect can finally fall away; the chapter joins a real warning to a real promise.

Before the end, ‘this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a testimony to all nations’ (verse 14). The waiting time is not empty; it is the time of witness, and the risen Jesus will send his disciples to make disciples of all nations until the end of the age (28:19-20).

The fall of the temple is presented as judgment on the city that rejected God's messengers (23:34-38), and the coming of the Son of Man brings a final sorting: one taken and another left, the faithful servant set over his master's possessions and the wicked one assigned a place with the hypocrites (verses 40 to 51). The judgment comes on those who were busy, not only on the notorious, since Noah's generation was simply eating, drinking, and marrying.

words.note: Parousia, presence, arrival. It occurs twenty-four times in the New Testament. It can mean simply someone's presence or coming (1 Corinthians 16:17, Philippians 2:12), but in the Greek world it was also the technical term for the visit of a ruler or official to a city, received with ceremony, as Adolf Deissmann showed from papyri and inscriptions (Light from the Ancient East). Matthew is the only Gospel to use it, four times in this chapter (verses 3, 27, 37, 39), and Paul, James, Peter, and John use it for Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:15, James 5:7, 2 Peter 3:4, 1 John 2:28). It became the church's standard word for the second coming.

Sunteleia, completion, consummation, end. It occurs six times in the New Testament, five in Matthew, always in the phrase ‘the end of the age’ (13:39, 13:40, 13:49, 24:3, 28:20), and once in Hebrews 9:26. The Greek of Daniel uses related phrases for the appointed end (Daniel 9:27, 12:13). It frames Matthew's teaching on the last things: the harvest at the end of the age in the parables, the disciples' question here, and the promise of Christ's presence ‘to the end of the age’.

Bdelugma, something detestable, an abomination. It occurs six times in the New Testament (here, Mark 13:14, Luke 16:15, and three times in Revelation). In the Greek Old Testament it often translates the Hebrew shiqquts and toevah, words for idols and idolatrous practices that defile what is holy. The phrase bdelugma tēs erēmōseōs, ‘the abomination that makes desolate’, comes from the Greek of Daniel (12:11, compare 9:27 and 11:31) and from 1 Maccabees 1:54, where it names the altar Antiochus IV set up in the temple. Matthew adds that it stands ‘in the holy place’ and names Daniel as its source.

Hupomenō, to remain, stand one's ground, endure. It occurs seventeen times in the New Testament, twice in Matthew, both in the same saying: ‘the one who perseveres to the end will be saved’ (10:22, 24:13). BDAG gives both to stay behind and to hold out under trial. It is not passive waiting but staying at one's post under pressure, the quality James praises in Job (James 5:11) and Hebrews in Jesus, who endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

Genea, generation, the people living at one time, and more broadly a family, race, or kind of people. It occurs about forty-three times in the New Testament and thirteen in Matthew, four of them in the genealogy (1:17). Elsewhere in Matthew it always means Jesus' contemporaries, usually with rebuke: ‘this generation’ like children in the marketplace (11:16), an evil and adulterous generation (12:39, 16:4), an unbelieving and perverse generation (17:17), and ‘this generation’ on whom the prophets' blood will come (23:36). Verse 34 depends on this word and on the phrase ‘all these things’, which is why interpreters argue about both.

Paralambanō, to take along, receive, take to oneself. It occurs about forty-nine times in the New Testament and sixteen in Matthew, often of taking someone into one's company or care: Joseph taking Mary as his wife (1:20, 1:24), taking the child and his mother (2:13-21), Jesus taking Peter, James, and John with him (17:1, 26:37). John uses it for Jesus' promise to take his disciples to himself (John 14:3). In verses 40 and 41 ‘one will be taken’ uses this verb; in the flood saying just before, the waters ‘swept them all away’ with a different verb (airō, verse 39). Whether the taken are gathered or removed in judgment is discussed under the hard questions.

Grēgoreō, to stay awake, keep watch. It occurs about twenty-two times in the New Testament and six in Matthew, all in this discourse (24:42, 24:43, 25:13) and in Gethsemane (26:38, 26:40, 26:41), where the disciples fail to do it. The standard lexicons give both the literal sense, to be awake, and the figurative sense of being alert and vigilant. In Matthew watching is not scanning the news for signs; it is faithfulness at an assigned post while the master is away, as the parable of the servant shows.

Dichotomeō, to cut in two. It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here and in Luke's parallel (Luke 12:46). Taken literally it describes a brutal punishment known in the ancient world (compare 1 Samuel 15:33 and Hebrews 11:37). Because the servant is then assigned a place with the hypocrites, and so is still alive, some interpreters take it figuratively; Otto Betz (Revue de Qumran, 1964) compared the Qumran curse that the unfaithful will be cut off from the midst of the sons of light (1QS 2:16-17). Either way, the image is of final separation from the master's household.

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the prophet greater than the prophets and as the Son of Man of Daniel 7. Like Jeremiah and Micah he foretells the fall of the temple, and his prediction came true within forty years. But he claims more than a prophet could. He warns that many will come in his name saying ‘I am the Christ’ (verse 5), which assumes that he alone may say it. He identifies himself with the one like a son of man who comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14), a claim he will repeat before the high priest (26:64). And he gives that figure the roles of Israel's God. In the Old Testament it is the LORD who gathers his scattered people from the four winds (Deuteronomy 30:4, Zechariah 2:6) and whose word stands forever (Isaiah 40:8); here the angels are ‘His angels’, the elect are ‘His elect’ (verse 31), and his words will never pass away (verse 35).

In the same breath he says that the Son does not know the day or the hour, only the Father (verse 36). The church has read this as part of the full reality of his humanity: the Son who shares the Father's being also shared, in his earthly life, the limits of human knowledge (Luke 2:52). The title ‘the Son’, set absolutely beside ‘the Father’ and above the angels, belongs to the highest Christology in Matthew (compare 11:27, 28:19), even in the sentence that states the limit. Athanasius and Gregory of Nazianzus explained the saying of his human nature, and the question is treated more fully in the notes on Mark 13.

The discourse is also a map of his own coming days. The one who warns that disciples will be handed over will himself be handed over (26:2); the one who speaks of false witnesses will face them (26:59-60); the one who commands watching will find his friends asleep. The mourning of the tribes in verse 30 echoes Zechariah's mourning for the one they pierced, and the New Testament hears in it the cross (John 19:37). The Son of Man who comes in power and great glory is the one who first goes to the cross, and Matthew's Gospel, which opened with the name Emmanuel, God with us (1:23), ends with the promise that he is with his people to the end of the age (28:20), the end the disciples asked about in verse 3.
interpretation:
The chapter has been read from the first centuries as history, hope, or both. The Didache (16), probably from the late first or early second century, already builds its closing warnings on it: false prophets multiplied, love turned to hate, lawlessness increasing, a world-deceiver working signs, then signs of truth and the Lord coming on the clouds. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.25, around 180) and Hippolytus (On Christ and Antichrist, around 200) read the abomination as the Antichrist in a rebuilt temple, the root of futurist reading. Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechetical Lectures 15.22, around 350) taught that the sign of the Son of Man in verse 30 is a luminous cross, and in a letter to the emperor Constantius he described a cross of light seen over Jerusalem in 351. Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 3.5-8) set Josephus's account of the siege beside Jesus' words to show them fulfilled, framing the city's fall as punishment of the Jews, a framing that shaped Christian attitudes for centuries. John Chrysostom (Homilies on Matthew 75 to 77, around 390) read the shortened days as God's mercy in cutting short the war and took this generation to mean the generation of believers. Jerome (Commentary on Matthew, 398) offered three readings of the abomination: the Antichrist, the image of Caesar that Pilate brought in, and Hadrian's statue on the temple site. Augustine (Letter 199, around 419) distinguished the fall of Jerusalem, the coming of Christ in his church, and the final coming, and refused to calculate the end. Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) held that Christ joined the destruction of Jerusalem and the last judgment in one discourse so that his disciples would live watchfully through both.

The modern labels grew from arguments over Revelation. The Jesuits Francisco Ribera (1590) and Luis de Alcázar (Vestigatio arcani sensus in Apocalypsi, 1614) proposed futurist and preterist readings against the Protestant historicism that identified the papacy with Antichrist. In the 1830s John Nelson Darby taught a secret rapture of the church before a future tribulation, spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), and Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), the film A Thief in the Night (1972) with Larry Norman's song I Wish We'd All Been Ready, and the Left Behind novels of Tim LaHaye and Jerry Jenkins (from 1995) made verses 40 and 41 the most famous picture of that rapture. Yet leading dispensational scholars such as John Walvoord (Matthew: Thy Kingdom Come, 1974) read those taken as taken in judgment at the second coming, while George Eldon Ladd (The Blessed Hope, 1956) and Robert Gundry (The Church and the Tribulation, 1973) argued for one coming after the tribulation. Preterist readings run from J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) and the partial preterism of R. C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus, 1998) to the critical-orthodox readings of N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) and R. T. France (The Gospel of Matthew, 2007), who place the turn to the final coming at verse 36; D. A. Carson (Expositor's Bible Commentary, 1984) and many others read a mixed pattern. Albert Schweitzer made the discourse the center of a Jesus who expected the end imminently.

In worship the chapter belongs to Advent. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 36 to 44 on the First Sunday of Advent in Year A, and the Roman lectionary verses 37 to 44. In Lutheran Leipzig verses 15 to 28 were the Gospel for the Twenty-fifth Sunday after Trinity, for which Bach wrote Es reißet euch ein schrecklich Ende (BWV 90, 1723).
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter. In verse 7 the King James Version reads ‘famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes’; ‘and pestilences’ is found in most later manuscripts but absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and a few others, and was probably added from Luke 21:11. In verse 31 the King James Version's ‘with a great sound of a trumpet’ reflects a longer reading in some manuscripts; the shorter text says simply ‘with a loud trumpet’. In verse 42 the King James Version reads ‘what hour your Lord doth come’, where the earliest manuscripts have ‘on what day’.

The most important variant is in verse 36. The words ‘nor the Son’ are found in Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and other early witnesses, but are missing from most later manuscripts, the Textus Receptus, and so the King James Version. Because they are secure in the parallel at Mark 13:32 and because scribes had a clear theological motive to remove them, editors are confident they belong in Matthew, and modern versions include them. In verse 15 Matthew makes ‘standing’ neuter, agreeing with the abomination, where Mark's masculine hints at a person (Mark 13:14).

A related variant lies in Luke. Many older Bibles print a Luke 17:36, ‘Two men shall be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left.’ It is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Luke and was borrowed from Matthew 24:40, which is why modern versions omit it there. In verse 28 English versions divide between ‘eagles’ (King James Version) and ‘vultures’ (most modern versions) for the same Greek word.

teach.big: Jesus prepares his followers for a world of upheaval, deception, and judgment not by giving them a timetable but by giving them his sure word and his promise to come, so that they refuse deception, endure to the end, bear witness to all nations, and are found faithful when he comes.

outline.t: What looks permanent is not: the most magnificent religious building of its age would fall, and the disciples' first instinct is to ask when rather than how to live.
The first danger is not war but deception; disasters are real, but they are birth pains, not proof that God has lost control or that the end has come.
Persecution, betrayal, false prophets, and cooling love will test the church, but the one who endures will be saved and the gospel will reach all nations.
When the crisis comes, faith flees rather than clings to the holy place: Jesus grieves for the vulnerable, tells his people to pray, and promises that God limits the days for the sake of his chosen.
Signs and wonders do not validate a messiah; Jesus has told us beforehand, and his coming will need no rumor to announce it.
History does not end in chaos but in the Son of Man, who comes with power and great glory and gathers his people from every corner of the earth.
The signs are real and his words are sure; Jesus' promises outlast the universe.
No one knows the day, not even the Son, and it will come on ordinary life as the flood came on Noah's generation, dividing people who stood side by side.
Because the hour is unknown, the only fitting posture is readiness, like a householder who would have stayed awake had he known.
Readiness is faithful work: the servant who feeds his fellow servants is blessed, and the one who presumes on his master's delay and abuses them is judged.

teach.pitfalls:
The commonest misuse of this chapter is to treat it as a code for dating the end, fitting each war, earthquake, or political event to a verse. Jesus says the opposite: these things must happen, ‘but the end is still to come’ (verse 6), and ‘no one knows about that day or hour’ (verse 36). Date-setters have always been wrong, and they have damaged the credibility of the gospel and the faith of those who trusted them. A second error runs the other way: explaining away the second coming because some of the chapter refers to AD 70. Even interpreters who read verses 29 to 31 of the temple's fall keep the personal return of Christ, which the creeds confess and verse 36 onward describes.

A third pitfall is to present one reading of verses 29 to 41 as the only faithful one. Preterist, futurist, and mixed readings, and pretribulational and posttribulational views of verses 40 and 41, are held by careful interpreters who share the church's confession, and a teacher should say so. A fourth is to preach verses 40 and 41 as if their meaning were obvious. The flood saying just before them makes those swept away the judged, so a teacher should at least show why many readers think it better to be left. A fifth is to read the temple's destruction as a verdict against the Jewish people. Jesus speaks as Jeremiah did, from inside Israel and with grief (23:37), and the same chapter warns his own followers that their love may grow cold and that a servant of Christ may be found beating his fellow servants.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on two kinds of fear. Some listeners were frightened by end-times preaching as children, came home to an empty house and thought they had been left behind, or still carry anxiety about missing the signs. They need to hear that Jesus' command is ‘see to it that you are not alarmed’ (verse 6) and that he told his disciples beforehand to steady them, not to terrify them. Others know the persecution and betrayal of verses 9 and 10 from experience: converts rejected by their families, believers who have lost work or safety for their faith, Christians from places where the church suffers. For them the promises that God shortens the days for the sake of the elect and that the one who endures will be saved are not abstractions. For the scrupulous, who fear they are not watching well enough, the parable's picture of watching is simply a servant doing the work he was given and caring for the others in the house.

hard.q: Jesus said this generation would not pass away until all these things happened. Was he mistaken about the time of his return?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. Verse 34 sets a time limit in the most solemn form Jesus uses, ‘Truly I tell you’, and in Matthew ‘this generation’ always means Jesus' contemporaries, most recently in 23:36, where it plainly does. Matthew sharpens the problem beyond Mark: the disciples ask about the sign of Jesus' parousia and the end of the age (verse 3), and the coming of the Son of Man follows ‘immediately after the tribulation of those days’ (verse 29). If ‘all these things’ includes that coming, Jesus predicted the end within his hearers' lifetimes, and it did not come. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in fragments published by Lessing in the 1770s, argued that the apostles' promise of an imminent return had simply failed, Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) built his portrait of Jesus as a prophet of the imminent end on sayings like this, and Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) cited the expectation against Jesus' wisdom. Jewish readers have added that the Messiah was to bring the age of peace the prophets foretold, and the world after Jesus did not see it.

Christian interpreters answer in three main ways. The preterist reading, argued by J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878), by R. C. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus, 1998), and in the moderate forms of N. T. Wright and R. T. France, holds that verses 4 to 35 describe the events leading to AD 70 and that the Son of Man's coming on the clouds uses Daniel 7's picture of the Son of Man coming to God to be vindicated and enthroned, displayed in the temple's fall, all within a generation; the final return is the subject of verses 36 onward. Full preterism, which places the final coming and the resurrection in the past, is rejected by these writers as contrary to the creeds. The futurist reading, common in dispensational teaching and represented by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), places much of the chapter still ahead and takes genea as the Jewish people or as the generation that sees the final signs begin. The mixed reading, represented by D. A. Carson (1984) and many commentators, notes that in the fig-tree saying ‘all these things’ are signs seen before the end, which tell that ‘He is near’ (verse 33), so ‘all these things’ in verse 34 need not include the coming itself; the temple fell within forty years, while ‘that day’ (verse 36) remains unknown. Each view carries a burden: the critical view must explain why Matthew kept and even sharpened a saying he knew had failed, the futurist must answer Matthew's consistent use of genea, and the preterist and mixed views must explain the closeness of verses 29 to 34. The timing of Christ's return is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ; that he will come is confessed by all.

hard.q: Does ‘one will be taken and the other left’ describe the rapture, and is it better to be taken or left?
hard.a:
For many Christians these verses are the clearest picture of the rapture: at a moment no one expects, believers are snatched away to meet Christ, and unbelievers are left behind to face a coming tribulation. That reading, taught by John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), became part of popular culture through Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth (1970), the film A Thief in the Night (1972), and the Left Behind novels (from 1995). Its defenders, among them pretribulational scholars such as John F. Hart, argue that verses 36 to 44 describe a coming that falls without warning on ordinary life, unlike the signs-heralded coming of verses 29 to 31, and so must be a separate event; that paralambanō is used of Jesus taking his own to himself (John 14:3); and that Paul describes believers being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Skeptical critics press a different objection: that the whole expectation, in any form, is a failed first-century hope.

Other readers answer from the passage itself. The saying comes directly after the flood, which ‘came and swept them all away’ (verse 39); by analogy, those taken are taken in judgment, and those left, like Noah, are spared. Luke's version adds the disciples' question ‘Where, Lord?’ and Jesus' answer about the vultures gathering at the body (Luke 17:37), which suggests death rather than rescue. For these reasons John Walvoord (Matthew: Thy Kingdom Come, 1974), himself a leading dispensationalist, read the taken as taken in judgment at the second coming, and many non-dispensational commentators agree. A third reading takes ‘taken’ positively but places it at the one visible coming of verses 30 and 31, when the angels gather the elect: this is the posttribulational view of George Eldon Ladd (The Blessed Hope, 1956) and Robert Gundry (The Church and the Tribulation, 1973), and it is close to the historic reading of Catholic, Orthodox, Reformed, and Lutheran interpreters, who see here the final separation at Christ's return without a separate rapture. What all these readers share is the passage's own point: people side by side in the same field and at the same mill will be divided by the coming of the Son of Man, and no one can tell beforehand by looking which is ready. The order of events is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ; the call to watch belongs to all of them.

observe: What three things do the disciples ask in verse 3, and what is the first thing Jesus says in reply?
List the warnings about deception in this chapter (verses 4 to 5, 11, 23 to 26). What do the deceivers claim, and how does Jesus say his own coming will differ?
In the parable of verses 45 to 51, what does the faithful servant do, and what does the wicked servant say in his heart?
interpret: How would you divide this chapter between the fall of the temple in AD 70 and the final coming of Christ? Which verses make the question hardest?
Why do you think Jesus compares his coming to the days of Noah, when people were eating, drinking, and marrying, rather than to a time of obvious wickedness?
What does it mean that even the Son does not know the day or hour, and how does that shape the way his followers should speak about the end?
apply: Verse 12 warns that the love of most will grow cold. What pressures cool love in you or your church, and what keeps it warm?
If readiness means being found doing your assigned work, what work has been entrusted to you, and what would faithfulness look like this week?
Has fear or fascination about the end times shaped your faith? How might Jesus' words ‘see to it that you are not alarmed’ change that?
